Having just shattered records by winning eight gold medals at the Beijing Summer Olympics, the American swimmer was celebrated as a national hero and the undisputed face of modern sports excellence. However, just months after his historic triumph, his pristine public image was thrown into turmoil by a single photograph.

In February 2009, the British tabloid *News of the World* published a photograph showing Phelps holding a glass pipe, commonly known as a bong, to his mouth. The picture had been secretly taken in November 2008 during a house party at the University of South Carolina in Columbia, where Phelps was visiting friends. The image went viral instantaneously, sparking an international media firestorm and calling into question the integrity of the world's greatest swimmer.

The incident quickly moved from a public relations nightmare to a potential legal issue when local law enforcement intervened. Sheriff Leon Lott of Richland County, South Carolina, known for taking a hardline stance on drug enforcement, launched a formal criminal investigation into the matter. Sheriff Lott acknowledged that while the photograph provided strong visual indication, it was not legally sufficient to prove what substance was inside the pipe or that a crime was committed in Richland County. 

Lott defended the decision to investigate the incident, which had drawn criticism from some who accused the department of wasting public resources to target a celebrity.

"Michael Phelps is an American hero, but he's also subject to the same laws as everyone else," Lott said. 

During the course of the investigation, police arrested seven people in connection with the party, mostly on drug possession and distribution charges, though none of those charges directly implicated Phelps.

In a statement released shortly after the sheriff's announcement, Phelps expressed relief that the ordeal was over and reiterated his regret over the incident.

"I'm glad this matter has been resolved and the decision has been made," Phelps said. "I made a bad judgment call and learned a valuable lesson from this experience. I'm looking forward to getting back in the pool and focusing on my goals."

The scandal has had mixed consequences for the swimmer, who achieved historic success at the 2008 Beijing Olympics by winning eight gold medals. 

Earlier this month, USA Swimming suspended Phelps from competition for three months and withdrew its financial support for that period, stating that while Phelps had not violated an anti-doping rule, his actions disappointed the organization and its members.

Phelps also suffered a financial hit when cereal giant Kellogg Co. announced it would not renew its endorsement contract with him, stating his behavior was "not consistent with the image of Kellogg." However, several major sponsors, including Speedo, Subway, and Omega, publicly stood by the athlete.

Phelps, 23, has since resumed training in Baltimore, Maryland, as he prepares for the 2009 World Championships later this summer and the 2012 London Olympics.
